newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - ROYALE BELGE.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - ROYALE BELGE.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Belgian insurance group Royale Belge's decision to pull out of reinsurance is being scrutinised for clues about its future.
Uncertainty over whether it will be retained or sold has hovered over Royale Belge since its parent UAP was acquired by Axa last year. Axa already has a Belgian unit, Axa Belgium.
At the end of May, Royale Belge chairman Jean-Pierre de Launoit told shareholders studies on the options were not finished.
"Whatever the solution is, it must favour the development of Royale Belge in line with the fundamental interests...of shareholders," de Launoit said.

The decision to quit reinsurance could be taken at face value. The company said its decision followed a review of the worldwide reinsurance market in which it had concluded there was little room for small players.
Certainly it is not about to become a world leader, and consolidation in reinsurance means its competitors are ever larger.

But reinsurance has always been a small part of the group's operation. More to the point, the company reported a 22.5 percent increase in reinsurance premiums in the first half of last year. Royale Belge Re said it had premium income of 6.9 billion Belgian francs in the whole of 1996 and made a profit of 386 million francs.
It could be that growth cannot be maintained because of other factors.

Belgium has some of the weakest controls over reinsurance companies in comparison with other countries, and there have been frequent calls for new controls. The issue is still a concern for both the market itself and politicians.

Another issue concerning reinsurance business in Belgium is the organisation of an insurance scheme covering floods and earthquakes, which requires their involvement. The scheme inspired by the French "CatNat" system, calls for a nine percent extra premium on all simple risks policies. Although there is potential for increased earnings, the risk portfolio may have appeared too wide.
Analysts will be looking at the decision to pare down operations to see if it makes Royale Belge a more attractive sales prospect.
There has been intense speculation on the Brussels bourse in that Royale Belge, and its 12.4 percent stake in bank BBL, were about to be sold, possibly to ING of the Netherlands.

ING has declined to comment, but Royale Belge's sale to ING would leave the Dutch group incontestably in control of BBL -- something it first aimed for in 1992 but failed to achieve. It would also make ING, which today announced the acquisition of U.S. life insurer Equitable of Iowa, a stiff insurance competitor for Belgian-Dutch insurance group Fortis.

Swiss insurance group Winterthur, which has links with Royale Belge through the Aviabel aviation insurance pool, has already denied reports that it is also a potential buyer. With the taste for acquisition in the market as strong as it is, doubtless other suitor would also appear.
